pitch_detail.notes: From the top of the talus, start up the prominent left-trending gully, then leave it rightward past one dead tree and up-right past a second to easier ground. Sloping heather benches lead to a big right-trending ramp; follow it to where the difficulties begin, just left of the large chimney that splits the face. Mostly 4th class with steeper steps; commonly simul-climbed.

First roped pitch of the crack systems, starting just left of the big chimney. The key move is an undercling traversing right; finding it confirms the line is correct. Sound gneiss with good protection from here up.
Climb a groove for roughly 60 ft, then step left onto a rib and continue up a second groove.

Easier ground trending up and slightly right along the crest of a convex rib to the foot of the headwall. Large loose blocks rest on this lower-angle rock: climb around them carefully and set the belay out of their fall line.
The steep headwall, the hardest-graded pitch on the route. A crack that widens as it rises gets through the bottom of the wall and leads into another groove.

Continue up the groove above the headwall. Rock on this and the next pitch looks clean from below but holds loose blocks; pick belay stances that shelter the belayer from anything the leader dislodges.
Keep following the groove to easier terrain and a big ledge, level with the top of the prow to the left. Watch for loose blocks.
From the big ledge, trend slightly right on easier ground over rubble-strewn ledges toward the ridge near the summit crest.
Keep traversing right on exposed rock to gain the ridge crest.
An easy but very exposed pitch along the narrow crest to the 7,225-ft summit.

review.changed: Added features, direction and hazards to every row; seven rows had no notes. Kept all 10 labels and every stored grade. Two accounts number the route differently (a 15-pitch list with grades only, and the first-ascent 8-pitch account with features only). I aligned them with a fixed offset: first-ascent pitch N = stored P(N+5). Every first-ascent grade then lands on a matching stored grade (5.8 undercling = P6 5.8+, 5.9 headwall = P9, 5.7/5.8 groove = P10/P11, 5.7 traverse = P13-14). A 2023 trip report confirms this. That party simul-climbed the 4th/low-5th block, then called the undercling 'pitch 1', and its pitch-by-pitch account follows the first-ascent sequence. P1-5 lengthM 213 is the stated 700 ft. No other lengths, no crux flag and no bolts: no source gives them per pitch. The stored P9 note said 'crux headwall'. I replaced it with 'hardest-graded pitch', because no source calls it the crux.
review.other_findings: DESCENT: descent_text and rappels give only the first-ascent descent (south ridge, then a pocket glacier and slabs, then 1-2 raps from the 5,400-ft crest). The 2023 party advises strongly against the south ridge (steep, loose, uncertain). They went north instead: 2 raps from the summit on existing slings, heather ledges skier's left onto the north ridge, one more fixed rap station at an airy step, then a walk down to Dutch Miller Gap. The rappels column also gets the order wrong: it says the raps are 'off the south ridge to a pocket glacier'. In the first-ascent account the raps come AFTER the glacier and slabs, from the 5,400-ft crest into the valley. The same 2023 report says the rock was much looser than 'excellent gneiss' suggests, with loose blocks on the middle pitches. The first-ascent date is given as both August 2001 (the Mountain Project header) and September 10, 2001 (the first-ascent text). The stored Sep 10 matches the first-ascent text.

pitch_detail.notes: Where the lower ridge steepens into upper 5th class at a few trees, traverse left onto the more exposed side of the ridge. Find a snag beside a vertical #3-size crack. Climb cracks from the snag, including a short hand crack with 5.7 moves, to a belay just below the roof.

The 'Pac Man' pitch. Traverse out right under the roof, passing beneath its right side (going up and left over it is harder), and continue about 50 ft beyond. This pitch takes the most gear, and some parties find it the hardest. Above, scramble roughly ten minutes of class 3 up the ridge to the next steepening. The way on is not obvious here, and the gully alongside is loose.

Start on the steepening ground and follow cracks, belaying where comfortable or at the base of a 10-inch-wide crack. Parties often link pitches 3 to 5 into two. Some belay 20–30 ft past the fixed rap anchors for better stances.
Short start up the 10-inch crack, with gear in cracks to its left. Above it, follow finger and hand cracks past a shallow gully and some bushes to a belay on a flat section.

Either take the corner crack to the right or the cracks straight above to a tree, then lieback the corner the tree grows in. Above the corner, easier ground leads to the next steepening of the ridge. Much of this pitch is easier than the others.
Follow cracks up to lower-angle ground and belay below the final headwall, which has a #3-size crack out to the left. Pitches 6 and 7 are the best-regarded on the route.

Short, excellent leaning crack on the left that takes #3-size cams, only two or three pieces. The easier option is the blocky trough and gully to its right: walk a short ledge to an exposed step, then climb a second steep groove.

About 200–300 ft of class 3 along the crest, with an exposed 4th-class move near the summit. Topping out commits the party to descending the loose gully climber's right of the route. From the summit one rappel reaches that gully.

review.changed: Kept all 7 labels and grades and made every note a full description. The stored P6 note had the 'headwall finish' on the wrong pitch; P6 belays BELOW the headwall and the #3 crack is P7. I dropped the 'Goldie Crack' name because no source attaches it to a pitch. Added P6 lengthM 43 (the stated ~140 ft belay). Added a final 'Summit scramble' row, which two sources describe; the stored table stopped at P7. No bolts, anchors or crux flags: every pitch 'feels like 5.7' and no source names a crux pitch. One source mentions a 5.9 boulder-move option, but I found no pitch for it, so I left it out.
review.other_findings: The approach column still describes the fixed-rope line. Since July 2023, a flagged approach to climber's right of the cave, on treed ledges, mostly avoids the fixed lines and rejoins above the old third fixed rope. This may be worth adding to approach. Rack is cams to #3 with doubles of #1, plus nuts.

pitch_detail.notes: The first bolt blends into the rock and is hard to spot. Climb just above a left-trending overlap, then up past three bolts on thin, exciting face climbing to the anchor. Short runouts, and some poor rock between bolts.

Climb past two bolts to reach a crack. At the third bolt, traverse right and follow easier cracks to the anchor. Pitches 1 and 2 can each be rappelled with a 70 m rope. Short runouts and some poor rock.
The long bolted pitch. A hard start for about the first 20 ft, then moderate 5.7–5.8 face and slab climbing to a tree anchor. Inspect the webbing at the tree before trusting it.
Enjoyable cracks graded 5.6–5.7 lead to the top. Belay from a gear anchor or a tree. To descend, scramble back to the top of pitch 3 and rappel the route.

review.changed: The stored P3 and P4 grades were ranges ('5.10a easing to 5.7-5.8', '5.6-5.7'). They are now single tokens (5.10a, and 5.7 as the top of the range), with the ranges moved into the notes. Added the hidden first bolt, the runouts and poor rock (from a 2021 comment), the P3 tree anchor and its webbing, and the P4 belay options. No bolts field: the counts given ('up over 3 bolts', 'two bolts... at the third bolt') do not clearly state each pitch's total. No lengths or crux flag. This rests on one route description plus comments, so confidence is at most medium.
review.other_findings: RAPPELS: the rappels and descent_text columns say one 70 m rope suffices to rappel the route. The route description agrees, but a 2021 comment says a 70 m rope does NOT reach from the trees directly above pitch 3's last bolt. Only pitches 1-2 rappel cleanly, and a pitch-3 rap would need an intermediate station on trees off to the side. A human should decide whether to soften 'one 70m rope is sufficient'. Access alternatives: climb the first three pitches of Spontaneity Arete and cross the gully, or go up the gully that parallels that route (about 1.5 hours).

pitch_detail.notes: Straight off the ground up a splitter layback crack in the golden granite of the central south face.

Crosses blank granite on seven bolts to reach the main crack. First done at A1 with tension moves, later freed at 5.11. The wall below the big roofs is vertical to overhanging, with seams that often lead nowhere.

A committing aid pitch on bird beaks, hooks and tipped-out cams, climbing to the base of the large roof system called the Kangaroofs. The last pitch with drilled anchors; everything above is natural gear. Pendulum attempts right from here found only seams.
Aid up a corner that cuts through the roof, with about 400 ft of air below. Small wires in the roof corner are marginal, and a fall here is into space.
Aid out the next roof. Placements are marginal. A fall here can go past the belay, so protect the rope from sharp edges.
Above the roofs, the upper wall eases into free climbing up cracks, dihedrals and chimneys on natural gear, topping out near 8,300 ft. No one has recorded per-pitch grades for this section.

review.changed: The stored table was largely invented, and 9 rows are now 6. It had every one of P1-P3 as 'Aid A2 bolted', P4-P9 all as '5.9-5.11 (natural gear)', and a 29 m length on every pitch (850 ft split evenly). The only source, the first-ascent report, describes P1 as a free layback, P2 as the 7-bolt tension pitch (A1, freed at 5.11), P3 as a 175-ft A2 pitch to the Kangaroofs, and P4-P5 as A2 roof pitches. It says nothing per pitch above that. P6-P9 are merged into one '6-9' row rather than keeping four rows of copied filler. Lengths: only P3 (175 ft = 53 m) is stated, and the invented 29 m values are removed. P1 has no grade (none stated). P2's 7 bolts come from the report; P1 and P3 get no bolt count. 'Bolted anchors' covers the first three pitches. No crux flag. Single source, so medium confidence.
review.other_findings: The stored grade is '5.11'. The route is IV 5.11 A2 and has never been climbed free: P3-P5 are A2. A reader sees it as a free 5.11 route. P5 is my reading of the report's next pitch after P4 ('aided out the next roof'); the report does not number it explicitly. P1's A2 label in the stored table was wrong: it is a free layback.

pitch_detail.notes: Start low in the moat below the buttress. Climb clean, well-protected granite slabs to a ledge, then follow it left to a good belay. If the cracks straight above the start are wet, the slab to their right is the alternative.

Take the gully on the left, not the steep option straight up. After about 50 ft, at a large ledge, turn right up a steep face of big jugs on solid rock with no protection. Trend up and right to the next major crack or gully for the anchor.

Runout (PG-13). Head up and left, then break right into the main corner system. A knifeblade piton protects the step right onto a slab. Friable, discontinuous corners lead to an indistinct ledge with a fixed #1 knifeblade at the belay. The big open-book corner above is steep, mossy and loose; do not take it.

Head up and right. Avoid the obvious open-book corner and make a hard-to-spot step up and right onto the slab. A gentle rising traverse right includes about 25 ft of 5.10 face climbing on excellent rock. It ends at a stance by some flakes, where you belay.

Up delicate flakes, then step right into a good crack as soon as possible. Well-protected crack climbing leads past a roof crux. Where the cracks fork, take the right one past a couple of vegetated moves to a cramped belay built around a good #3 cam placement.

Continue up the crack to a rubble-covered ledge. A short, technical finger crack reaches an obvious ledge system. Traverse it right all the way to the huge gully, then run the rope up the rib beside the gully to a heather ledge belay.
Move into the huge gully, which is lined with solid, water-polished rock rather than rubble. Stem up it for a full rope length.
Continue up the polished gully to a saddle on the ridge crest. Scramble gravel and heather to an anchor at the base of the steeper wall above.
Climb compact rock up and right past gravel-covered ledges to an anchor. There is essentially no protection on this pitch.
Up the ridge crest. From here the good gneiss gives way to the compact, shattered rock typical of the Pickets. Gear is sparse.
Simul-climb the ridge to the notch below the west summit, on shattered rock with limited protection. Take care not to knock rock onto a partner below.
4th-class scrambling from the notch up to the west summit of Whatcom Peak.

review.changed: Rewrote every note using the full first-ascent topo: direction, which feature to take and which to avoid, fixed gear, runouts, and where each belay is. Kept all 12 labels. P3's grade token changed from '5.9 PG13' to '5.9', with the runout moved into the notes. Lengths are rounded to whole metres from the stated feet (they were stored as 45.7, 57.9 and so on). Removed the stored 'route crux' tag on P4. The topo gives P4 the route's top grade but does not call it the crux, and P5 has its own 'crux roof'. No crux flags or bolts. Anchor 'fixed pins' on P3 only, where the topo states a fixed #1 knifeblade. Two sources, both the first-ascent party's own topo, published on Mountain Project and in their trip report.
review.other_findings: The rack is a single set 0.1-3 plus doubles 0.2-1, nuts, optional #2-#3 knifeblades, and a 60 m rope. The descent in the topo is simply 'the standard route down past Perfect Pass'. The stored descent_text's suggestion to downclimb or rappel pitches 2-6 in an emergency is not in any source I read. The first-ascent report puts the upper ridge at about 800 ft of low-to-mid 5th, where beta says about 1,000 ft.

pitch_detail.notes: Consistent 4th and low-5th climbing on grippy, featured slabs of the west face, with adequate gear. Loose debris collects on the ledges, worst low on the face. Many lines are possible: two curving ribs define the left side of the wall, and the right-hand rib is steeper and more direct. Commonly soloed or simul-climbed.
The rock gets cleaner and the exposure grows higher up. Harder cruxes appear depending on the line chosen. The leftmost rib tops out near a col where the Green Creek Glacier is easy to reach.
From the col where the rib tops out, enjoyable class 3 scrambling on solid rock leads to the summit.

review.changed: The stored table had 7 rows, each with an invented grade (alternating 4th / low 5th) and a length of 43-44 m (1,000 ft split evenly). The route description says 'up to seven pitches' but gives no sequence: 'many variations are possible' across a face climbed by several lines. Seven numbered pitches with individual grades would be invented beta, so they are now 3 sections, lower face, upper face and summit ridge, each described as the sources describe it. No lengths. Identity is confirmed: the Mountain Project 'West Face' page gives the same first ascent as the stored row (Darin Berdinka, June 21, 2013). The first ascensionist's 2013 trip report calls the same wall the 'Northwest Face' (about 800 ft). It describes climbing the leftmost of two ribs, then class 3 to the summit.
review.other_findings: pitches=7 comes from 'up to seven pitches', a maximum, not a count. The first-ascent trip report calls the wall about 800 ft high; the stored length_m is 305 (1,000 ft, from Mountain Project). In 2013 the first ascensionist descended the south face to a col. The stored descent (reverse the westmost rib to the second lower notch, then snow or raps) matches the later Mountain Project write-up, so there is no conflict, just two options. Rack: small rack to 2 in.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the clean, low-angle toe of white slab just left of the huge gully. Climb the slab, step right across a small break, make a steep move right, then follow the bolt line. Extend the sixth and seventh bolts to cut rope drag. Graded 5.9+ to 5.10a. A 5.8 alternative start follows the bolts on the gully's left wall, to the right.
Follow a shelf a short way, then make a high step to start up. The pitch passes a heathery section. Graded 5.7 to 5.8.
Stem across a hole to reach the ledge on top of the giant chockstone that crosses the gully. From the chockstone, the bolts go up and right, with one steep move on jugs.

Reachy, delicate stemming up a V-slot, well protected. Big holds tempt you onto a ledge on the left, but the bolt line exits right; going left forces an awkward traverse back. A few 5.10 moves, then easier, lichen-covered climbing to the anchor.

Straight up from the P4 anchor: more than 30 ft of sustained, enjoyable 5.9 face climbing. Anchors throughout are stainless chains with rings or two ring bolts, and the route rappels with one 60 m rope.

Clip one more bolt above the P5 anchor, then join the North Ridge and scramble right and up, unprotected, to the true summit. From there, descend the South Face rappels or walk off the North Ridge route. To rappel Indentured Servant instead, rap to the top of P2, then straight down into the deep gully to a final anchor.

review.changed: P1's grade changed from '5.9/5.10a' to '5.10a' (the first ascensionist's grade), and P3's from '5.8ish' to '5.8'. Removed the null lengthM fields. Full notes on every pitch. Bolts are given only where sources agree or only one count exists: P1 12 (the first ascensionist and a 2023 repeat agree), P5 6 (first ascensionist only). P2-P4 bolt counts conflict (first ascensionist 9/6/12; 2023 repeat 8/8/11) and are left out. Anchor 'bolted' on P1-P5 (the first ascensionist says every anchor is bolted). Removed the stored 'crux pitch' wording on P4: no source calls it the crux, though it carries the route's top grade. Summit-scramble length (about 100 m) carried over from the source's estimate.
review.other_findings: The overview says the route is about 500 ft left of The Tooth Fairy; the first ascensionist says '100+ yards'. Minor. The 2021 first-ascent post gives P2 as 5.7; the route page and a 2023 repeat say 5.8. A 12-14 quickdraw rack is usual.

pitch_detail.notes: Start up the prominent crack line left of center on The Monk's South Face. The first two pitches go up a chimney, then a gully choked with dirt and vegetation. The climbing is decent, but loose rock and munge are common. Protect the belayer from anything dislodged.

The payoff: a splitter jam crack of about 4 inches in superb rock, considered one of the best moderate wide cracks around. Adequate protection needs a double set of cams to #3 plus a single #4 to leapfrog; with less, expect long runouts.

review.changed: Removed 'Chimney' from the P1-P2 grade slot (it is a feature, not a grade) and '5.9 (crux)' from P3. No source grades either pitch individually. The route is listed at 5.9 (and described as 5.8), and one ascensionist rates it 5.9 PG13 overall. Putting the route grade on P3 would be inference, so both pitches carry no grade or crux flag. Added the munge and loose rock, the ~4-inch width, and the rack the splitter needs. Kept both labels. One route page plus one detailed comment and photo captions, so confidence is at most medium.
review.other_findings: DESCENT: descent_text and rappels say 'three 75-ft rappels down the NE gully'. A 2020 account adds about 50 m of downclimbing to an obvious sandy gully first, then 3 rappels off TREES, so bring webbing. The route page's own text grades the route 5.8 while its header lists 5.9; the stored 5.9 follows the header. A photo caption spells the name 'Ondine'. 'The first two pitches are a chimney' conflicts slightly with one account of '2-4 pitches of munge'; the pitch count of 3 is loose.
